author: jacobsklug
text:
Claude Code loops are simpler than everyone makes them sound.

I broke down every piece across real builds and live testing.

Here's the full system:

1/ What a Loop Is
> A recurring task that keeps running until the job is done
> Not a one-shot prompt. Not a pipeline. A persistent agent with a goal.
> It checks completion after every pass and decides whether to stop or go again

2/ How It Differs From a Routine
> A routine is linear. Step 1, step 2, step 3, done. Think Zapier.
> A loop is circular. It finishes a pass, checks its goal, and starts again if needed
> Routines stop. Loops stop only when the end state is met.

3/ What Makes Up a Loop
> Goal: the north star the entire loop works toward
> Prompts: the instructions for each pass
> Tools: whatever Claude needs to actually do the work
> Memory: context carried between passes
> End state: the specific condition that kills the loop

4/ Loop Rules
> Minimum frequency: every 1 minute
> Hard limit: 3 days max before everything stops
> Cost reality: every pass burns tokens. 10-minute loops over 3 days adds up fast.
> Keep prompts tight. Vague loops = expensive loops.

5/ Use Case 1: PR Review Loop
> /loop every 10 minutes
> Review every new pull request. Check diff for bugs and regressions. Fix what you find. Commit back to the same PR.
> End state: tests pass, lint is clean, CI is green.

6/ Use Case 2: Internal Tool From Spec
> /loop every 10 minutes
> Read the spec doc. Build the next missing piece. Write tests for it.
> End state: every item in the spec is built and all tests pass.
> You set it, walk away, and come back to a working app.

The whole point of loops: stop babysitting your AI.

Define the goal. Define done. Let it run.

The best engineers aren't prompting harder. They're looping smarter.

text:
【サイバーセキュリティ動向分析】

今日（2026年6月26日）の主なサイバーセキュリティニュースについて、主要トピックごとに背景・影響・対策を詳しくまとめます。情報は直近の公開情報に基づき、進行中の脅威やパッチ対応を中心に取り上げています。
1. ShinyHuntersによるOracle PeopleSoft大規模侵害キャンペーン（継続中）
背景
サイバー犯罪グループ「ShinyHunters」（GoogleのMandiantではUNC6240として追跡）が、Oracle PeopleSoftのPeopleTools環境管理コンポーネントに存在する重大な脆弱性（CVE-2026-35273、CVSS 9.8）をゼロデイとして悪用した大規模キャンペーンが確認されました。攻撃活動は5月27日から6月9日頃まで活発で、Oracleが6月10日に緊急セキュリティアドバイザリを発行するまでパッチが提供されていませんでした。この脆弱性は認証不要でリモートコード実行（RCE）が可能という極めて危険なもので、主にインターネットに公開されたPSEMHUBエンドポイントを標的にしていました。ShinyHuntersは教育機関を中心に100以上の組織（数百のインスタンス）を侵害し、学生・教職員の個人情報（氏名、住所、メール、誕生日、民族、GPA、専攻、学生IDなど）を大量に窃取したと主張しています。
影響
高等教育機関を中心に世界中の組織が被害を受け、個人情報の大量流出と恐喝行為が発生しています。窃取データがShinyHuntersのリークサイトで公開・販売される動きが見られ、被害組織の評判低下、規制対応コストの増大、さらなる二次被害（フィッシングやアカウント乗っ取り）のリスクが高まっています。教育セクターは特に機微な個人情報を大量に扱うため、社会的影響が大きいです。また、Oracleのエンタープライズソフトウェアが広く使われていることから、サプライチェーン的な波及も懸念されます。
対策  
Oracleのセキュリティアドバイザリに従い、PeopleTools 8.61および8.62向けのパッチを最優先で適用してください。サポート対象外の古いバージョンも早急に更新または廃止を検討。
インターネット公開されているPeopleSoftインスタンスの露出を最小限に抑え、WAF（Web Application Firewall）の導入やネットワークセグメンテーションを実施。
異常なネットワークトラフィックや認証ログを監視し、Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligenceなどの脅威インテリジェンスを活用。
データ暗号化、最小権限の原則、定期的な脆弱性スキャンと侵入テストを徹底。侵害が疑われる場合は直ちに専門機関に相談。
2. Anthropicの先進AIモデル「Claude Fable 5」および「Mythos 5」のアクセス停止（6月12日頃）
背景
Anthropicが6月9日頃に公開した最先端AIモデル「Claude Fable 5」と「Mythos 5」に対し、米国政府（商務省）が輸出管理当局に基づく国家安全保障上の指令を発出しました。主な懸念は、これらのモデルが「jailbreak（脱獄）」されることで、サイバー脆弱性の特定・悪用に悪用される可能性です。指令では外国人の利用制限が求められ、Anthropicはコンプライアンスのため世界中の全ユーザーに対して一時的にアクセスを停止しました。他のモデル（例: Opusシリーズ）は影響を受けていません。
影響
AI開発・利用の現場に大きな混乱をもたらしています。企業や研究機関が先進AIを活用した業務やイノベーションが一時停止を余儀なくされ、AIガバナンスの重要性が改めて浮き彫りになりました。AIがサイバー攻撃の加速要因となるリスク（脆弱性発見の自動化など）が現実のものとして認識され、国際的なAI規制議論が活発化しています。AnthropicをはじめとするAI企業は、セキュリティとイノベーションのバランスに苦慮する状況です。
対策  
現時点では代替モデルや自社内製AI、または制限付きの旧バージョンを使用。
AIツールの利用ポリシーを策定し、jailbreak対策（プロンプトガードレール、出力監視）を強化。
政府・規制当局との連携を強化し、輸出管理や安全基準に準拠したAI運用を徹底。
企業はAI導入時のリスクアセスメントを必須とし、機微な業務での使用を制限。長期的に「安全なAI開発フレームワーク」の構築が求められます。
3. Microsoft 2026年6月 Patch Tuesdayの大規模パッチリリース（6月9-10日頃）
背景
Microsoftが6月の月例パッチで過去最多規模となる206件以上の脆弱性を修正しました（Critical 37件以上）。中には3件の公開済みゼロデイ脆弱性も含まれており、Windows、Office、Azure、Visual Studio Code、IISなど幅広い製品に影響します。ゼロデイの例として、IISのサービス拒否（DoS）やVisual Studio CodeでのGitHubトークン窃取などが挙げられます。パッチ数は過去最高を更新し、ソフトウェアの複雑化と脆弱性発見の加速を象徴しています。
影響
未パッチのシステムが攻撃者に狙われやすく、特にゼロデイは公開直後から悪用リスクが高まります。企業・政府機関では業務中断やデータ漏洩の可能性が現実的です。一方で、迅速なパッチ適用により多くの攻撃を未然に防げます。全体として、サイバー脅威の「量と質」の両方が高まっている状況を示しています。
対策  
パッチをできるだけ早くテスト・展開（特にCriticalとゼロデイ）。自動パッチ管理ツールを活用。
脆弱性管理プログラムを強化し、優先順位付け（CVSSスコア、公開 exploit の有無）を徹底。
パッチ適用までの緩和策として、ネットワーク分離や多要素認証（MFA）、エンドポイント検知・対応（EDR）の強化を実施。
定期的なパッチ適用テスト環境の整備と、緊急時の対応計画の見直しを推奨。
4. AIコーディングエージェントを標的とした「Agentjacking」攻撃の新手法（6月12日頃公開）
背景

影響
開発者のワークステーションが直接乗っ取られるリスクが生じ、ソフトウェア開発サプライチェーン全体に影響を及ぼす可能性があります。AIエージェントの普及が進む中、信頼できる外部データソースが攻撃ベクトルになるという新しい脅威形態です。検知が難しく、既存のセキュリティ制御をすり抜けやすい点が深刻です。
対策  
SentryなどのツールとAIエージェントの統合を制限または監視強化。入力データのサニタイズを徹底。
AIエージェントの実行権限を最小限に抑え、サンドボックス環境で運用。
AIエージェントの出力・行動を常時ログ監視し、異常なコマンド実行を検知する仕組みを導入。
開発者教育を強化し、「AIが信頼する外部情報」のリスクを周知。ツールの最新版への更新を徹底。
その他の注目動向（6月下旬時点）
Lantronix EDS5000の脆弱性（CVE-2025-67038）：CISAが積極的な悪用を警告。OT環境向けシリアル-to-IP変換器で、6月26日までのパッチ適用を強く推奨。
GitLabのパッチリリース：コード実行や情報漏洩を含む13件の脆弱性を修正（高深刻度含む）。
Cisco Catalyst SD-WANのゼロデイ（CVE-2026-20245）：数ヶ月前から悪用されていたことが判明。
マルウェア対策の進展：AmadeyおよびStealCのインフラが法執行機関とセキュリティ企業により大規模に破壊され、数千万件の認証情報が回収。
AI関連では、プロンプトインジェクションを悪用したmacOSマルウェア「Gaslight」（北朝鮮関連疑い）なども報告されています。
これらのニュースは、AIの両刃の剣化、パッチ管理の重要性、サプライチェーン・開発環境への攻撃シフトという共通のトレンドを示しています。組織はパッチ適用を最優先とし、AIツールの利用ポリシーを早急に整備するとともに、脅威インテリジェンスの活用と多層防御を強化してください。状況は日々変化するため、最新の公式情報を継続的に確認することをおすすめします。

影響
AI開発・利用の現場に大きな混乱をもたらしています。企業や研究機関が先進AIを活用した業務やイノベーションが一時停止を余儀なくされ、AIガバナンスの重要性が改めて浮き彫りになりました。AIがサイバー攻撃の加速要因となるリスク（脆弱性発見の自動化など）が現実のものとして認識され、国際的なAI規制議論が活発化しています。AnthropicをはじめとするAI企業は、セキュリティとイノベーションのバランスに苦慮する状況です。

現時点では代替モデルや自社内製AI、または制限付きの旧バージョンを使用。
AIツールの利用ポリシーを策定し、jailbreak対策（プロンプトガードレール、出力監視）を強化。
政府・規制当局との連携を強化し、輸出管理や安全基準に準拠したAI運用を徹底。
企業はAI導入時のリスクアセスメントを必須とし、機微な業務での使用を制限。長期的に「安全なAI開発フレームワーク」の構築が求められます。
3. Microsoft 2026年6月 Patch Tuesdayの大規模パッチリリース（6月9-10日頃）
背景
Microsoftが6月の月例パッチで過去最多規模となる206件以上の脆弱性を修正しました（Critical 37件以上）。中には3件の公開済みゼロデイ脆弱性も含まれており、Windows、Office、Azure、Visual Studio Code、IISなど幅広い製品に影響します。ゼロデイの例として、IISのサービス拒否（DoS）やVisual Studio CodeでのGitHubトークン窃取などが挙げられます。パッチ数は過去最高を更新し、ソフトウェアの複雑化と脆弱性発見の加速を象徴しています。

未パッチのシステムが攻撃者に狙われやすく、特にゼロデイは公開直後から悪用リスクが高まります。企業・政府機関では業務中断やデータ漏洩の可能性が現実的です。一方で、迅速なパッチ適用により多くの攻撃を未然に防げます。全体として、サイバー脅威の「量と質」の両方が高まっている状況を示しています。

text:
U.S. frontier APIs now have release-risk and access-risk. Serious AI/biotech researchers should treat local/open-weight capacity as resilience infrastructure, not a hobby. Chinese open-weight models are currently among the strongest practical options, but the winning stack should be plural, audited, reproducible, and biosecurity-aware—not simply “run Chinese models.”

1. Reality check: “controlled rollout” is directionally true, but not yet a formal licensing regime

The U.S. government has not openly created a blanket “AI model license” system. The June 2026 White House order explicitly says its frontier-model section does not authorize mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting for developing, publishing, releasing, or distributing AI models. But the same order also creates a voluntary early-access framework where developers can give the government access to “covered frontier models” for up to 30 days before release to trusted partners, and collaborate with the government on who those trusted partners are. That is why “de facto control” is a fair political reading, even if “formal pre-release licensing” is not yet legally precise.

The GPT-5.6 reporting makes this much more concrete. Axios reported that the Trump administration asked OpenAI to initially limit GPT-5.6 to a small group of government-approved partners before wider rollout, citing national-security concerns; Reuters similarly reported that Sam Altman told staff GPT-5.6 would be released first to select partners with government approval handled customer by customer.

The Anthropic case is an even stronger signal that model access can become a national-security/export-control object. Anthropic says the U.S. government ordered it to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by all foreign nationals, including some Anthropic employees, and that Anthropic disabled access for all customers in response. Anthropic also argued that the directive lacked specific evidence and warned that applying that standard broadly would halt deployment of advanced models.

So the mental-model update is:

Old assumption:
Frontier APIs are commercial products that vendors release when ready.

New assumption:
Frontier APIs are strategic dual-use assets whose rollout, customer access, employee access, and geography may be shaped by government pressure, export controls, trusted-partner programs, and classified evaluations.

2. The post is right about local/open, but “open source” needs precision

A lot of people say “open source model” when they mean “open weights.” The Open Source Initiative’s Open Source AI Definition expects enough access to understand, use, modify, and share the system, including model parameters, relevant code, and information about training data. OSI separately warns that “open weights” share final parameters but often do not provide the full training code, dataset, or data-transparency needed for full reproducibility.
That distinction matters for AI/biotech research:
Open weights are enough for:
local inference
fine-tuning
privacy
vendor independence
offline continuity
latency control
some reproducibility

True open source is needed for:
scientific auditability
training-data provenance
bias analysis
safety review
derivative training confidence
regulatory-grade documentation

The practical answer is not “only use true open source,” because many powerful models are not fully open in that sense. The practical answer is to classify models honestly:

Tier A: fully open scientific stack
weights + code + data recipe + permissive license

Tier B: open-weight operational stack
weights + inference code + usable license, but incomplete training transparency

Tier C: hosted API stack
no weights, no local control, strongest capabilities but highest access risk

Tier D: black-box regulated stack
access mediated by government/vendor/region/customer approvals

For research continuity, you want a portfolio across these tiers, with local Tier A/B as the base layer.
3. Why Chinese open-weight models matter now
Chinese open-weight models have become impossible to ignore. Qwen’s official repository says Qwen3 open-weight models are released under Apache 2.0 and support tool use through Qwen-Agent, vLLM, SGLang, Transformers, llama.cpp, and Ollama-style local workflows.
DeepSeek-R1’s model card says the code and weights are MIT-licensed, with commercial use, modification, derivatives, and distillation permitted, subject to notes around distilled models.
https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s GLM-5.2 is another example of the direction of travel: its repo describes a 1M-token-context model family aimed at coding and long-context tasks, with local serving support through SGLang, vLLM, Transformers, KTransformers, Unsloth, and Ascend NPU tooling. Reuters reported that https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F framed GLM-5.2 as narrowing the gap with top closed models while being adapted for domestic Chinese chip infrastructure.
The strategic point: Chinese labs are not merely copying U.S. closed-model behavior. They are competing through open-weight distribution, cost efficiency, local deployability, long context, permissive licensing, and sovereign hardware adaptation. Reuters reported that a U.S. advisory body warned Chinese open-source models could create a self-reinforcing advantage, and cited estimates that many U.S. startups already use Chinese open-source AI models.
But do not overcorrect into a new monoculture. “Mostly Chinese models” is a good wake-up call, not a complete strategy.
The stronger version is:

Use Chinese open-weight models aggressively,
but do not become dependent on any single country, lab, license, repository, model family, serving stack, or censorship prior.

4. The real goal: inference sovereignty
The key concept is inference sovereignty.
Not just:
Can I download a model?

But:
Can I run it when APIs are restricted?
Can I run it on my own data without leaking it?
Can I reproduce old results six months later?
Can I swap models without rewriting my workflows?
Can I audit the model supply chain?
Can I keep doing research if a vendor, country, cloud, or regulator says no?

For AI/biotech researchers, the correct architecture is local-first but not local-only:

Local/open models:
baseline research continuity, private data, coding, paper RAG, reproducibility, internal agents

Closed frontier APIs:
optional accelerators, external critique, high-end reasoning, comparison, red-team review

Specialized scientific models:
structure prediction, sequence modeling, docking/affinity triage, literature extraction, data cleaning

Deterministic tools:
BLAST-like search, molecular simulation, unit tests, statistical checks, databases, notebooks, workflow managers

Do not let any chat model become the scientific authority. The model should propose; tools and evidence should dispose.

5. Practical local/open stack for AI + biotech research
Layer 1: Local model gateway

Build one internal endpoint that routes requests to multiple models.
Research question → router → model choice → tool permissions → audit log → output validator

Example model roles:
Qwen / DeepSeek / GLM:
general reasoning, coding, agentic workflows, long-context synthesis

Smaller quantized models:
offline drafting, summarization, private notes, cheap iteration

Specialized bio models:
structure/affinity/genome/sequence tasks

Closed frontier models:
optional external reviewer, not system of record

Use a serving layer that can support multiple backends. vLLM emphasizes high-throughput serving, prefix caching, quantization, structured outputs, tool calling, OpenAI-compatible APIs, and support for many model families including Qwen and DeepSeek. SGLang similarly emphasizes low-latency/high-throughput serving, prefix caching, multi-GPU parallelism, OpenAI-compatible APIs, and support for Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, TPU, and Ascend hardware.

For smaller local deployments, GGUF is important because it is designed for efficient inference in llama.cpp-style runtimes and is used by tools such as llama.cpp, LM Studio, GPT4All, and Ollama.

Layer 2: Local scientific RAG

Your local model should not rely on memory for science. Give it a private retrieval system over:

papers
preprints
patents
grant text
lab notes
negative results
datasets
protocol documentation
SOPs
regulatory documents
model cards
internal benchmarks

Every answer should carry citations and a confidence label:

Known from retrieved source
Inferred from retrieved source
Speculative hypothesis
Requires wetlab/computational validation
Out of scope / unsafe / not enough evidence

For biotech research, this is critical because a fluent model can produce plausible but false scientific claims. The model should be forced to quote its evidence trail, generate testable hypotheses, and separate “literature-supported” from “novel speculation.”

Layer 3: Scientific tool sandbox
Do not let an agent run arbitrary shell commands on your real machine.
Use a sandbox pattern:

read-only literature corpus
ephemeral container
no network by default
limited file mounts
explicit package allowlist
logged commands
resource limits
separate secrets vault
human approval for external calls

For coding-heavy AI/biotech work, local agents are useful only when they are surrounded by deterministic checks:

unit tests
type checks
notebook reruns
dataset checksums
statistical sanity checks
reference baselines
version-locked environments
reproducibility reports

Layer 4: Specialized bio models

Do not treat general LLMs as substitutes for scientific models.
For protein structure and binding-affinity triage, Boltz is a strong open scientific stack to track. The Boltz repo describes Boltz-1 as a fully open-source model approaching AlphaFold3-level biomolecular structure prediction, and Boltz-2 as jointly modeling complex structures and binding affinities, with code and weights released under MIT for academic and commercial use.
For genomics, Evo 2 is a major model to understand, but it also illustrates why biosecurity controls matter. Arc Institute describes Evo 2 as a genome foundation model trained on trillions of DNA tokens across more than 128,000 genomes, with public code and weights, long-context genomic modeling, and capabilities relevant to disease-mutation prediction and genome design.
The safe research pattern is:
Use specialized bio models for legitimate analysis, interpretation, triage, and hypothesis generation.
Do not rely on general-purpose chat models for protocols, pathogen engineering, immune evasion, or operational wetlab design.
Route high-risk biological requests through institutional review and biosecurity screening.

Layer 5: Biosecurity airlock

Local models remove vendor-side safeguards. That is useful for privacy and continuity, but it also means your lab must supply its own safety layer.

NIST notes that synthetic nucleic acid technologies are dual-use and that AI may enable design of novel sequences that evade existing screening approaches, which is why it is developing scalable and verifiable screening mechanisms. U.S. health-security guidance has also linked federal funding conditions to procurement from compliant nucleic-acid synthesis providers and preventing access to sequences of concern without legitimate need.
A good biotech AI stack needs an internal “airlock”:

Low risk:
literature review, coding, data cleaning, structure visualization, benign assay interpretation

Medium risk:
novel protein design, gene editing analysis, large-scale sequence generation, wetlab planning

High risk:
pathogens, toxins, virulence, host-range changes, immune escape, synthesis-ready constructs, evasion of screening

Disallowed without formal institutional approval:
actionable assistance for enhancing pathogenicity, evading detection, bypassing synthesis controls, or enabling biological harm

This is not moral theater. It is operational risk management.

6. Supply-chain security: the part most people will skip and regret
Running your own model is not automatically safer. You are downloading giant executable-ish artifacts from the internet.

Hugging Face’s security documentation warns that Pickle-based model files can execute arbitrary code during loading, and recommends safer approaches such as safetensors, trusted sources, signed commits, and avoiding unsafe deserialization. Hugging Face’s enterprise security guidance also treats safetensors, malware scanning, and avoiding unverified custom code as important model eligibility controls.
Minimum model supply-chain checklist:

Download only from official orgs or verified mirrors.
Prefer safetensors over pickle-based formats.
Pin exact model revisions and commit hashes.
Record license, checksum, source URL, quantization source, and conversion script.
Avoid trust_remote_code unless reviewed.
Scan model repos and auxiliary code.
Run new models in a sandbox before production use.
Keep a model SBOM: model bill of materials.
Maintain frozen known-good checkpoints.
Re-evaluate after every model, quantization, or serving-stack update.

For AI/biotech research, add:
Track which model generated which hypothesis.
Track which model processed which sensitive dataset.
Track whether clinical, genomic, proprietary, or unpublished data touched any hosted API.
Store reproducibility metadata with every notebook and paper draft.

7. “Genius-level” solutions

A. Build a Frontier Exit Plan

Assume a closed frontier model can disappear, degrade, get rate-limited, become region-blocked, or become unavailable to foreign-national teammates.

Create a continuity table:
Task                          Primary        Local fallback       Quality floor
Literature review             GPT/Claude      Qwen/DeepSeek/GLM    citation recall > X
Code generation               GPT/Claude      Qwen coder/GLM       tests pass
Bio paper extraction          closed API      local RAG + Qwen     extraction F1 > X
Protein triage                Boltz/closed    Boltz local          benchmark recovery > X
Genomic interpretation        Evo/ESM/tools   local specialized    expert review required
Grant drafting                any LLM         local model          human review
Internal data analysis        local only      local only           no hosted API

The point is not to make local models always best. The point is to make them sufficiently good and always available.
B. Create a Local Model Router with a capability ledger

Do not manually choose models forever. Build a router that knows:
model name
version
license
context length
cost
latency
hardware requirement
coding score on your tasks
literature extraction score
biosecurity risk rating
known censorship/ideology quirks
tool-use reliability
date last evaluated
allowed data sensitivity

Then route like this:
Sensitive internal data → local only

1. Reality check: “controlled rollout” is directionally true, but not yet a formal licensing regime

The U.S. government has not openly created a blanket “AI model license” system. The June 2026 White House order explicitly says its frontier-model section does not authorize mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting for developing, publishing, releasing, or distributing AI models. But the same order also creates a voluntary early-access framework where developers can give the government access to “covered frontier models” for up to 30 days before release to trusted partners, and collaborate with the government on who those trusted partners are. That is why “de facto control” is a fair political reading, even if “formal pre-release licensing” is not yet legally precise.

The GPT-5.6 reporting makes this much more concrete. Axios reported that the Trump administration asked OpenAI to initially limit GPT-5.6 to a small group of government-approved partners before wider rollout, citing national-security concerns; Reuters similarly reported that Sam Altman told staff GPT-5.6 would be released first to select partners with government approval handled customer by customer.

The Anthropic case is an even stronger signal that model access can become a national-security/export-control object. Anthropic says the U.S. government ordered it to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by all foreign nationals, including some Anthropic employees, and that Anthropic disabled access for all customers in response. Anthropic also argued that the directive lacked specific evidence and warned that applying that standard broadly would halt deployment of advanced models.

So the mental-model update is:

Old assumption:
Frontier APIs are commercial products that vendors release when ready.

New assumption:
Frontier APIs are strategic dual-use assets whose rollout, customer access, employee access, and geography may be shaped by government pressure, export controls, trusted-partner programs, and classified evaluations.

OSI separately warns that “open weights” share final parameters but often do not provide the full training code, dataset, or data-transparency needed for full reproducibility.

Open weights are enough for:
local inference
fine-tuning
privacy
vendor independence
offline continuity
latency control
some reproducibility

True open source is needed for:
scientific auditability
training-data provenance
bias analysis
safety review
derivative training confidence
regulatory-grade documentation

Tier A: fully open scientific stack
weights + code + data recipe + permissive license

Tier B: open-weight operational stack
weights + inference code + usable license, but incomplete training transparency

Tier C: hosted API stack

A solo dev posted a GTA 6 prototype built with Claude 4 in 48 hours.

The media thought that was the story. It was not.

The real story was the server logs. No Unity license. No Unreal Engine splash. No Rockstar proprietary middleware. The map was procedurally generated from a single prompt. The physics ran on a lightweight WebGL build. The NPC behavior was Claude calling itself every 200ms through a local Ollama instance.

The AI stack: Claude 4 for architecture and game logic ($40 API credit), a single RTX 4090 for inference ($1,600), ComfyUI for texture generation ($0 in cloud cost), and a free Vercel deployment. Total hardware/API cost under $2,000. Rockstar's GTA 6 budget is reportedly over $2 billion.

The market gives 0% odds Anthropic IPOs by June 30, 2026 -- because no one believes Claude's creator can go public within a month. Yet a single developer using that same model just eliminated a $2 billion labor barrier and a decade of production time in a long weekend.
